lead: Both readings are about true and false teachers. Paul fears that the Corinthians, betrothed to Christ, will be led astray by smooth preachers who bring “another Jesus”. In John, Jesus teaches in the Temple, and the people wonder where his learning comes from; he answers that his teaching is not his own but the Father’s, and asks them to judge rightly, not by appearances. The test of a teacher is not eloquence or credentials but whether he seeks the glory of the One who sent him.

set: Chapters 10–13 of 2 Corinthians are Paul’s sharpest words to this Church. Since his last letter, preachers have arrived at Corinth who boast of their speaking skill and of letters of recommendation, and who look down on Paul as weak and unimpressive in person (10:10). Paul calls them, with irony, “super-apostles”. To defend the Gospel he must now speak about himself, which he calls a kind of foolishness.
str: v. 1: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness.
vv. 2–3: his divine jealousy: he has betrothed them to Christ and fears they will be seduced as Eve was.
v. 4: they accept another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel all too easily.
vv. 5–6: he is not inferior to the super-apostles; untrained in speech, but not in knowledge.
kw: The jealousy of God himself, who loves his people as a husband loves his bride and will not share them with idols (Hosea 2:19–20). Paul shares God’s own protective love for the Church.

In Jewish custom the betrothal was already binding; the bride was then led to the bridegroom’s house. Paul sees himself as the friend who arranged the betrothal and must present the bride faithful on the wedding day, the Lord’s coming.
Literally “the over-much apostles”. Paul mocks their self-importance. True apostleship is measured by faithfulness to Christ crucified, not by impressive speech.
vv: I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
The whole Church, and each soul, is the bride of Christ. Faithfulness to the Gospel is faithfulness in love.
as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
Error rarely comes as plain evil. Like the serpent, it comes with clever words and makes the truth seem small.
I may be untrained in speech, but not in knowledge
Paul may have lacked the polished style that the Greeks admired, but he did not lack the knowledge of Christ. The Gospel does not depend on rhetoric.
ch: The Catechism draws on this verse when it teaches that the Church is the bride of Christ: the Apostle speaks of the whole Church and of each of the faithful as a bride betrothed to Christ the Lord, to become one spirit with him (CCC 796). The Church has always heard in Paul’s fear a warning against changing the Gospel: there is not “another Jesus”, but the one handed on by the apostles. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, notes that Paul calls his concern jealousy because it burns with love for them, not for himself (in substance, Homilies on 2 Corinthians).

set: Jesus has gone up to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 10), the joyful autumn harvest feast when people lived in shelters made of branches. Opinions about him are divided, and the authorities are seeking to kill him (7:1). In the middle of the feast he teaches openly in the Temple. The “one work” he speaks of is the healing of the man at the pool of Bethesda on a sabbath (5:1–18), which had first stirred the authorities against him.
str: vv. 14–15: Jesus teaches in the Temple; they wonder at his learning.
vv. 16–18: his teaching comes from the Father; whoever wants to do God’s will will recognize it.
vv. 19–20: none of you keeps the law; why seek to kill me? The crowd: “You have a demon!”
vv. 21–24: the argument from circumcision on the sabbath; judge with right judgment.
kw: Literally “letters”: the learning of one trained under a teacher of the Law. Jesus had not studied in a rabbinic school, yet he taught with authority.
Jesus does not claim a teaching of his own invention. As the Son he speaks what he has received from the Father (12:49).
Literally “according to the face”, by what is seen on the surface. Right judgment looks to the purpose of the Law and the heart of God.
vv: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me.
This is not modesty but a statement of who he is. The Son’s teaching is the Father’s teaching, because the Son is one with the Father (10:30).
Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God
Knowing the truth about Christ is not only a matter of study. Those who set themselves to obey God come to recognize his voice.
If a man receives circumcision on the sabbath in order that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I healed a man’s whole body on the sabbath?

A boy is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3) even if it falls on a sabbath; later Jewish teachers also recorded this rule. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if one rite of the covenant may be done on the sabbath, how much more may a whole person be made well.
Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.
The words are for every age. We easily judge by outward signs; God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
ch: St Augustine asks how the teaching can be both “mine” and “not mine”, and answers that the Son is himself the Word of the Father: what is the Father’s teaching but the Word? He also takes verse 17 as a rule for faith: understanding is the reward of faith; do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe so that you may understand (in substance, Tractates on John 29). In John, “the Jews” in verse 15 means the Temple authorities and their circle in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as such; Jesus, his disciples and the crowd were all Jews, and the Church warns against any reading that blames the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

study: Paul fears that the Corinthians may accept “another Jesus”. What images of Jesus in today’s culture differ from the Jesus of the Gospel and the Church?
Jesus says, “Do not judge by appearances.” Whom have I judged by appearances this week, and how can I look again with right judgment?
